far.name: MoM-z14
far.why: The most distant galaxy whose redshift has been measured from its spectrum (as of October 2026): we see it as it was 280 million years after the Big Bang. Webb found it in the COSMOS field. It is tiny, half its light coming from within about 240 light-years of its centre, and very bright.
far.source: Naidu and others 2025, 'A Cosmic Miracle: A Remarkably Luminous Galaxy at z_spec = 14.44 Confirmed with JWST', arXiv:2505.11263 (abstract and Table 1: R.A. 150.0933255, Dec. 2.2731627, z = 14.44 +-0.02, 280 million years after the Big Bang, circularized r_e = 74 pc; read 2026-10-28)

far.name: JADES-GS-z14-0
far.why: A galaxy seen about 300 million years after the Big Bang. Webb found it; the ALMA telescopes then detected oxygen in it, an element stars make, and measured its redshift to four decimals.
far.source: Carniani and others 2024, Nature, arXiv:2405.18485 (Table 1: JADES-GS-z14-0 at 3:32:19.905, -27:51:20.27; NIRSpec redshift 14.32 +0.08 -0.20); Carniani and others 2025, A&A, arXiv:2409.20533 (ALMA [OIII] 88 micron line, z = 14.1796 +-0.0007, UV magnitude -20.81, half-light radius 260 pc; read 2026-10-28)

far.name: GN-z11
far.why: Hubble found it in 2015 and Webb confirmed it: a galaxy seen 400 million years after the Big Bang. In 2024 astronomers reported a black hole in its centre, then the earliest known.
far.source: Oesch and others 2016, ApJ 819, 129, arXiv:1603.00461 (Table 2: R.A. 12:36:25.46, Dec. +62:14:31.4); Bunker and others 2023, A&A 677, A88, arXiv:2302.07256 ('z = 10.60'); Maiolino and others 2024, Nature, arXiv:2305.12492 (z = 10.603, a black hole in its centre; read 2026-10-28)
